lessons.title: What AI, machine learning, generative AI and agentic AI actually are
lessons.outcome: Distinguish rules-based automation, predictive machine learning, generative AI and agentic AI, and classify an insurance tool correctly.

blocks.text: Core ideas

"Artificial intelligence" is used loosely in the industry, and most of the confusion professionals face comes from treating very different technologies as one thing. The unit therefore teaches four categories that learners can use to classify any tool a vendor, manager or colleague describes.

Rules-based automation follows instructions written explicitly by people: "if the vehicle is older than fifteen years, refer the proposal to a senior underwriter." It is predictable and easy to audit, but it cannot handle situations its authors did not anticipate and it does not learn. Robotic process automation (RPA) is a common form of this, where software repeats the clicks and keystrokes a person would make across systems.

Machine learning (ML) builds a model from historical data rather than from hand-written rules. A model trained on several years of motor claims can produce a score estimating how likely a new claim is to need investigation. ML is predictive: it classifies, scores or forecasts. Its quality depends entirely on the data it learned from, so gaps or biases in historical records carry forward into its predictions.

Generative AI (GenAI) produces new content, text, images, summaries, translations, code, based on patterns learned from very large datasets. Large language models (LLMs) are the generative systems most professionals now meet, through assistants that draft letters, summarise reports or explain policy wording. Their output is fluent but probabilistic, which means it can be confidently wrong.

Agentic AI uses a generative model as a "reasoning engine" that can plan several steps towards a goal, use tools (search a policy database, read an email, call a pricing system, send a message) and adjust its plan based on results. The difference from a chatbot is action: a chatbot answers, an agent does things. The IAIS notes that agentic AI is one of the new developments accelerating AI adoption in insurance (S07).

blocks.text: Regulation and practice

No Ugandan law defines these categories, but the distinction matters in practice because the risks differ. Rules are transparent; ML scores may be hard to explain to a customer whose claim is delayed; generative output may contain fabricated facts; agents can take actions that bind the company. The Data Protection and Privacy Act 2019 contains a right relating to automated decision-taking (S05, section to be confirmed), which becomes relevant as soon as an ML model or agent makes or heavily shapes a decision about an individual.
Scenarios from Ugandan insurance
These scenarios are illustrative. They have not yet been checked against interviews with practitioners.

A bancassurance relationship manager at a Kampala bank is told by a vendor that their new "AI underwriting engine" will speed up credit-life approvals. On questioning, it turns out to be a rules table, useful, but not AI that learns, and it will need manual updating whenever the insurer's underwriting guidelines change.

A medical insurer's claims team adopts a GenAI assistant to summarise hospital invoices. One summary lists a procedure that does not appear on the invoice. The team realises the tool generates plausible text rather than extracting facts, and adds a check against the source document.
Common mistakes

Calling every automated system "AI", which hides important differences in risk; assuming GenAI "looks up" answers rather than generating them; assuming an agent is safe because each individual step seems harmless; and believing AI will replace professional judgment, when current practice shows insurers keep humans in charge of material decisions (S10).
Techniques to use

Teach the "four-question classifier": Does it follow fixed rules written by people? Does it learn from historical data to predict? Does it create new content? Does it take actions using tools? The first "yes" from the top gives the main category, and a tool may combine several.
Where it helps and where it fails
Applications span every function, but each category has a characteristic limitation: rules are brittle, ML inherits data bias, GenAI fabricates, agents compound errors across steps.

lessons.title: How large language models work, and why they get things wrong
lessons.outcome: Explain in plain terms how an LLM produces answers and predict the situations in which it is likely to be unreliable.

blocks.text: Core ideas

An LLM is trained on a very large body of text to predict the next piece of text, a "token", roughly a word or part of a word, given everything before it. By repeating this prediction many times it produces sentences, paragraphs and documents. It does not consult a database of verified facts unless it has been connected to one; it produces the most plausible continuation based on patterns in its training.

Several practical consequences follow. **Hallucination** (NIST uses the term "confabulation", to be confirmed S08) is the production of fluent, confident content that is false or unsupported, a non-existent IRA circular, an invented clause number, a wrong premium calculation. The **knowledge cutoff** means the model's built-in knowledge stops at a training date, so recent regulation, new product rules or this year's tariff changes may be missing unless the tool can search or the user provides the text. The **context window** is how much text the model can consider at once; very long documents may be truncated or details in the middle may receive less attention. **Non-determinism** means the same prompt can give different answers on different attempts. **Arithmetic and counting** are weak points for language models working without a calculator tool. **Language coverage** varies: performance in English is usually stronger than in Luganda, Runyankore or Swahili, so translations of policy wording need native-speaker review.

Tools connected to search, document retrieval or company systems ("grounding" or "retrieval") reduce but do not eliminate these problems. A tool that claims to have "checked the IRA website" when it has no browsing capability is generating text, not reporting an action.
Regulation and practice

An insurer remains accountable for what it tells customers regardless of whether a person or a model drafted it. Misstatements about cover, exclusions or claim timelines can amount to poor market conduct. The IAIS paper's transparency and explainability topic (S07) expects firms to understand and be able to explain AI-driven outcomes.
Scenarios from Ugandan insurance
These scenarios are illustrative. They have not yet been checked against interviews with practitioners.

An underwriting assistant asks an AI tool for "the current IRA requirements for motor third-party insurance" and receives a confident answer citing a circular number that cannot be found. The assistant learns to ask for the source text and to check the IRA website directly.

A customer service officer asks a tool to translate a funeral-cover exclusion into Luganda for a customer; a colleague who speaks Luganda notices the translation reverses the meaning of "not covered".
Common mistakes

Treating the AI as a search engine; trusting citations without opening them; using AI-computed premiums, sums insured or settlement figures without recalculating; pasting a 150-page policy and assuming every clause was considered; assuming a polished answer means a correct one.
Techniques to use

Provide the source text and ask the model to answer only from it and to quote the clause it relied on; ask the model to state what it is unsure of; recalculate every number independently; break long documents into sections; use native-speaker review for any customer-facing translation.
Where it helps and where it fails
Strong at drafting, restructuring, summarising provided text, generating options and explaining concepts. Weak at recent facts, exact citations, arithmetic without tools, and rare or local knowledge.

lessons.title: The AI opportunity across the insurance value chain
lessons.outcome: Map AI applications to each stage of the insurance value chain and judge which are realistic for the Ugandan market today.

blocks.text: Core ideas

The insurance value chain runs from product design and pricing, through distribution and sales, underwriting, policy administration and servicing, to claims, fraud management and recoveries, with finance, compliance and reporting running alongside. AI can contribute at each stage, but value is concentrated where work is high-volume, document-heavy and repetitive, and where faster or more consistent decisions directly affect cost or customer experience.

blocks.text: Regulation and practice

The legal requirement to settle claims within a set period after complete documentation (reported as 60 days, S03; *verify section in S04*) gives claims automation a clear compliance motive. Any use case processing personal data must comply with DPPA 2019 (S05). Distribution use cases through banks involve two regulated parties and both sets of conduct expectations.
Scenarios from Ugandan insurance
These scenarios are illustrative. They have not yet been checked against interviews with practitioners.

A mid-sized general insurer receives most motor claim notifications through WhatsApp and phone calls. Missing documents are the main cause of delay. An AI-assisted intake checklist that tells the customer exactly what is still missing is a low-risk, high-value first use case.

A life insurer growing through bancassurance wants relationship managers to explain products consistently. A GenAI tool drafting plain-language explanations from approved product sheets, reviewed by compliance, reduces mis-selling risk.
Common mistakes

Starting with the most impressive use case rather than the most valuable and safest; copying a foreign insurer's use case without checking local data quality and connectivity; measuring success by "using AI" rather than by cycle time, cost, complaint rates or customer satisfaction; ignoring the cost of change management and training.
Techniques to use
Prioritise use cases with a simple screen: high volume, repetitive, document-heavy, measurable, low harm if wrong, and data available. Start where AI assists a person rather than decides.
Where it helps and where it fails
Applications are broad; limitations in Uganda include connectivity, cost, paper-based records, language diversity and limited historical data for model training.

modules.title: Working with generative AI in daily insurance work

lessons.title: Prompting for insurance tasks
lessons.outcome: Write structured prompts that produce usable first drafts for common insurance tasks.

blocks.text: Core ideas

A prompt is the instruction and material given to an AI model. Because the model generates the most plausible continuation of what it receives, vague prompts get generic answers and well-structured prompts get specific, usable ones. The Academy teaches a five-part structure, **RCTCF**: **Role** (who the AI should act as, e.g., "a claims communication specialist at a Ugandan general insurer"), **Context** (the facts of the situation, the audience and any source material), **Task** (exactly what to produce), **Constraints** (what to avoid, length, tone, what must be included, "use only the text provided"), and **Format** (letter, table, bullet summary, WhatsApp message under 300 characters). Two further techniques lift quality: giving an **example** of the desired output, and asking the model to **ask clarifying questions** before drafting. Prompting is iterative, the first draft is refined through follow-up instructions ("make it warmer", "remove the jargon", "add the documents still outstanding").

Prompting is not a way to make the model accurate about facts it does not have. It improves structure, tone and relevance; accuracy still depends on providing correct source information and verifying the result (Unit 2.2).
Regulation and practice

Prompts themselves can contain personal data; Unit 2.3 governs what may be included. Templates for prompts that will be reused across a team should be approved, stored centrally and versioned like any other procedure.
Scenarios from Ugandan insurance
These scenarios are illustrative. They have not yet been checked against interviews with practitioners.

Weak prompt: "Write a letter about a delayed claim." Strong prompt: "You are a claims communication specialist at a Ugandan general insurer. A customer's motor own-damage claim is delayed because the police abstract has not been received. Write a WhatsApp message under 120 words, in plain English, that apologises for the wait, explains exactly which document is outstanding and where to get it, gives the claims officer's direct line, and does not promise a settlement date. Use a respectful, warm tone."

Underwriting: "Using only the valuation report text pasted below, produce a table of property address, construction type, sum insured recommended, and any risk features mentioned. Write 'not stated' where the report does not say. Do not infer."
Bancassurance: "Explain the credit-life cover in the approved product sheet below to a small-business borrower in five short sentences, avoiding insurance jargon. Include the main exclusion."
Common mistakes

One-line prompts with no context; asking for facts the model cannot know; not stating the audience; forgetting to forbid invented details; accepting the first draft; including customer identifiers unnecessarily.
Techniques to use
Use RCTCF; paste source text and tell the model to use only it; specify "write 'not stated' rather than guessing"; ask for clarifying questions; keep a team library of tested prompts.
Where it helps and where it fails
Good for drafting letters, messages, summaries, comparisons, training materials and meeting notes. Not a substitute for knowledge of the specific policy, the customer's file or current regulation.

lessons.title: Verifying AI output before you use it
lessons.outcome: Apply a systematic check to AI output to catch factual, numerical, coverage and tone errors.

blocks.text: Core ideas

The professional, not the tool, is accountable for anything sent to a customer, broker, bank partner or regulator. The Academy teaches a three-part verification routine, the **3C check**. **Correct**: every fact, name, date, policy number, clause reference and figure matches the source, numbers are recalculated independently, never "confirmed" by asking the same AI. **Complete**: nothing material is missing, exclusions, conditions, outstanding documents, deadlines, the customer's right to complain or escalate. **Compliant**: the output respects data protection, does not promise what the company has not decided, does not misstate cover, and uses an appropriate tone for the customer's situation (for example, a death claim).

Two further concepts help. **Automation bias** is the tendency to accept machine output because it looks authoritative, especially under time pressure; the antidote is a fixed checklist used every time. **Proportionate review** means the depth of checking matches the stakes: an internal meeting summary needs a quick read; a repudiation letter needs line-by-line verification against the file and policy wording.
Regulation and practice

Statements to customers about cover and claims are conduct matters under the Insurance Act and IRA oversight (S04, to be confirmed). Errors in documents sent to a bank partner can create liability for both parties. Firms should record which outputs were AI-assisted and who verified them, supporting the accountability principle in S07.
Scenarios from Ugandan insurance
These scenarios are illustrative. They have not yet been checked against interviews with practitioners.
An AI-drafted settlement letter states a sum of UGX 4,850,000; the claims file shows UGX 4,580,000 after excess. The digits were transposed when the officer pasted figures; the 3C check catches it.

A summary of a medical policy for a corporate client omits the waiting period for maternity cover. The "Complete" check against the policy schedule catches it before the HR manager circulates the summary to staff.
Common mistakes

Checking only spelling and tone; asking the AI "is this correct?"; skipping verification under time pressure; trusting citations without opening them; reviewing the AI output without reopening the source.
Techniques to use

Keep the source document open beside the draft; highlight every number and recompute; tick off a completeness list specific to the document type; read the output once from the customer's perspective; record the verifier's name for customer-facing documents.
Where it helps and where it fails
AI can help verification by, for example, listing every figure in a draft so a person can check each, but the check itself must be against the source by a person or a deterministic tool.

lessons.title: Protecting personal data when using AI
lessons.outcome: Decide what information may and may not be entered into an AI tool, and apply the DPPA 2019 principles to AI use.

blocks.text: Core ideas

Insurance runs on personal data: names, national identification numbers, phone numbers, addresses, vehicle registrations, medical records, bank details, beneficiary information. Uganda's Data Protection and Privacy Act 2019 (DPPA) applies to the collection, processing, holding or use of personal data within Uganda, and to processing outside Uganda of data relating to Ugandan citizens (S05, S06). Its supporting Regulations were gazetted in March 2021, and the Personal Data Protection Office (PDPO), under NITA-U, has been operational since August 2021 (S06). Every data collector, processor and controller must register with the PDPO (S06). The Act sets out principles of data protection, requires consent for collection and processing subject to exceptions, restricts processing of special personal data, sets conditions for processing personal data outside Uganda, and gives data subjects rights including rights in relation to automated decision-taking (S05). Where processing is likely to threaten data subjects' rights, a data protection impact assessment is expected before processing begins (secondary summary; *verify against the Regulations*).

For AI use, four questions guide every professional. **Is personal data needed for this task?** Most drafting and summarising can be done with names and identifiers removed or replaced. **Where does the data go?** Many public AI tools process data on servers outside Uganda and may retain or use inputs, which engages the DPPA's conditions for processing outside Uganda. **Is the tool approved?** The organisation, not the individual, should decide which tools may handle which data, based on contract terms and security (S18). **Is the processing consistent with the purpose for which data was collected?** Data collected to process a claim should not be repurposed for marketing via AI without a lawful basis.

Key practical terms: **anonymisation** (removing identifiers so the person cannot be identified), **pseudonymisation** (replacing identifiers with codes, e.g., "Claimant A"), **special personal data** (categories requiring extra protection, the DPPA list includes health-related information; *verify the full list*), and **data minimisation** (use only what is needed).
Regulation and practice

The DPPA creates offences including unlawful obtaining or disclosure of personal data and sale of personal data (S05). Insurers' data protection officers should be involved in approving AI tools. Commentators argue the DPPA does not yet address algorithmic profiling and AI-specific impact assessments in detail (S15), so firms should apply the existing principles conservatively.
Scenarios from Ugandan insurance
These scenarios are illustrative. They have not yet been checked against interviews with practitioners.

A claims officer pastes a full medical report, including the patient's name and national ID, into a free public AI tool to summarise it. The same summary could have been produced with "Patient A", no ID and only the clinical sections needed.

A broker wants to use AI to draft renewal reminders using the full client list exported from the CRM. The safer approach is to draft one template with placeholders and merge personal details inside the broker's own system.
Common mistakes

Pasting complete customer files; assuming deleting the chat removes the data from the provider; using personal accounts on public tools for work; sharing screenshots of AI chats containing customer data on messaging groups; repurposing claims data for marketing.
Techniques to use

Strip or replace identifiers before using AI; use templates with placeholders; use only organisation-approved tools for any personal data; keep special personal data (especially medical information) out of public tools entirely; ask the data protection officer when unsure.
Where it helps and where it fails
AI can help detect personal data in documents before sharing, but such checks must themselves be tested. AI tools cannot make an unlawful processing activity lawful.

modules.title: Agentic AI: from assistants to agents

lessons.title: What makes a system agentic
lessons.outcome: Describe the components of an AI agent and place a given system on an autonomy scale.

blocks.text: Core ideas

An AI agent combines five components. A **goal** sets what it is trying to achieve ("get this claim file complete and ready for assessment"). A **reasoning model**, usually an LLM, interprets the goal and plans steps. **Tools** let it act: reading emails, querying the policy administration system, checking a payment status, sending a WhatsApp message, creating a task. **Memory** keeps track of what has happened so far in the task and sometimes across tasks. **Guardrails** define what the agent may and may not do, permissions, spending or value limits, topics it must refuse, situations where it must hand over to a person.

A useful distinction is between a **workflow** (a fixed sequence of steps in which an AI model performs some of them) and an **agent** (which decides for itself which steps to take and in what order). Many practical "agentic" deployments in insurance are closer to workflows with AI steps, which is often the safer design.

The Academy uses a five-level **autonomy scale**: Level 0, suggests only (human does everything); Level 1, drafts outputs for human use; Level 2, prepares and proposes actions that a human approves one by one; Level 3, acts automatically within defined limits and escalates exceptions; Level 4, acts fully autonomously. Industry tracking in 2026 shows insurers using agents mainly to summarise, route and accelerate work, with few giving agents material authority over pricing, coverage or claims decisions (S10), that is, most real deployments sit at Levels 1 to 3.
Regulation and practice

The more autonomy an agent has, the more the firm's governance must cover its actions as if they were taken by an employee: authority limits, records, supervision and the ability to stop it. Agents acting on personal data engage the DPPA, including the right relating to automated decision-taking (S05).
Scenarios from Ugandan insurance
These scenarios are illustrative. They have not yet been checked against interviews with practitioners.

A general insurer's "claims agent" receives a WhatsApp message reporting a minor accident, checks the policy is in force, lists outstanding documents, sends the customer the checklist, and creates a claim file for a human officer. It cannot approve or decline anything. This is Level 2 to 3 for intake and Level 0 for decisions.
A bancassurance "agent" prepares a renewal reminder for each expiring credit-life policy and queues it for the relationship manager to send, Level 2.
Common mistakes

Assuming "agent" means "fully autonomous"; describing a fixed workflow as an agent (or vice versa) when assessing risk; granting broad tool access "for convenience"; forgetting that agents can chain small errors into a large one.
Techniques to use
Describe any proposed agent by listing its goal, tools, memory and guardrails, then assign an autonomy level separately for each type of action it can take.
Where it helps and where it fails
Agents excel at multi-step, repetitive coordination tasks. Limitations include compounding errors, vulnerability to manipulated inputs (Unit 3.3) and difficulty handling genuinely novel situations.

lessons.title: Agentic use cases in claims, underwriting, distribution and service
lessons.outcome: Evaluate an agentic use case for value, feasibility and risk in a Ugandan setting.

blocks.text: Core ideas

Each use case is evaluated on three axes. **Value**: volume, time saved, leakage reduced, customer experience, compliance with settlement timelines. **Feasibility**: data availability and quality, digital versus paper documents, integration with core systems, connectivity, language. **Risk**: impact on customers if wrong, personal data involved, autonomy level required, ability to explain outcomes.

In Uganda, specific features matter: claims and enquiries commonly arrive by phone and WhatsApp; many documents are paper or photographed; payouts may go to mobile money; and IRA attention to settlement timeliness (S03) gives intake and document-chasing agents a strong case.
Regulation and practice

Fraud flags must not become automatic denials: flagged claims need investigation and fair treatment. Any agent communicating with customers must not misstate cover or promise outcomes. Agents processing health data (medical claims) carry heightened data protection obligations (S05).
Scenarios from Ugandan insurance
These scenarios are illustrative. They have not yet been checked against interviews with practitioners.

A Kampala motor insurer pilots an intake agent on WhatsApp. Average time from notification to complete file falls, but the agent misreads handwritten police abstracts. The team keeps the agent for checklists and reminders but routes all handwritten documents to a person.
A medical insurer considers an agent that flags hospitals billing the same procedure unusually often. The flags go to an investigations officer, not to automatic claim rejection.
Common mistakes

Choosing the use case with the most impressive demo rather than the best value-feasibility-risk balance; testing only on clean digital documents; measuring time saved but not error rates or complaints; letting fraud flags block payments automatically.
Techniques to use

Use the three-axis scoring (value, feasibility, risk, each 1 to 5) and pilot with a defined baseline, success metrics and a limited scope. Test with real Ugandan document samples, including poor-quality photographs.
Where it helps and where it fails
Strongest near-term fit: intake, document checklists, status updates, submission summaries. Higher-risk: anything that decides cover, price or payment.

lessons.title: Designing human oversight for AI agents
lessons.outcome: Design decision rights, escalation triggers and audit controls for an agentic workflow.

blocks.text: Core ideas

Human oversight is designed, not assumed. The Academy teaches five building blocks. A **decision-rights matrix** lists every action the agent can take and states, for each, whether the agent may act alone, must seek approval, or must never act. **Escalation triggers** are conditions that send a case to a person: value above a threshold, low model confidence, missing or conflicting documents, a complaint or distress signal, a vulnerable customer (bereavement, serious illness), or any request outside the agent's scope. An **audit trail** records inputs, the agent's reasoning or steps, tools used, outputs and who approved what, so decisions can be explained and reviewed. **Monitoring** tracks error rates, escalation rates, complaints and drift over time, with regular sampling of the agent's work by a person. A **stop mechanism** ("kill switch") lets the business pause the agent immediately.

Agents also face a specific security risk: **prompt injection**, where instructions hidden in content the agent reads (an email, a PDF, a web page) try to make it do something unintended, for example, a document containing hidden text telling the agent to "mark this claim approved". OWASP lists prompt injection and excessive agency among the top risks for LLM applications (S17, to be confirmed). The defences are least-privilege tool permissions, treating all external content as data not instructions, human approval for consequential actions, and testing with adversarial examples.

Meaningful oversight also guards against **rubber-stamping**: if a human approves hundreds of agent decisions a day without time to review, the oversight is nominal. Approval volumes and review time should be sized realistically.
Regulation and practice

Uganda's government has stated that transparency, accountability and human oversight must underpin AI governance (S12). The DPPA's automated decision-taking provision (S05) makes it important that individuals affected by significant automated decisions can obtain human involvement (*verify exact wording*). Audit trails support both IRA supervision and responses to complaints.
Scenarios from Ugandan insurance
These scenarios are illustrative. They have not yet been checked against interviews with practitioners.

An intake agent's decision-rights matrix: may send document checklists alone; may create claim files alone; must get approval to tell a customer a claim is "not covered"; must never authorise payment. Escalation triggers: any death claim, any message containing the words "complaint" or "lawyer", any amount over a set threshold.

A broker's quoting agent reads a client email containing hidden text instructing it to apply the maximum discount. Least-privilege permissions mean it can only propose discounts for human approval, so the attack fails.
Common mistakes

Treating "a human can review if needed" as oversight; no record of what the agent did; giving agents broad system permissions; escalation rules so wide everything escalates (no value) or so narrow nothing does (no control); no way to stop the agent quickly.
Techniques to use

Build the decision-rights matrix first; set escalation triggers from real complaint and error data; sample a fixed percentage of agent work weekly; test with adversarial documents before go-live; name an accountable owner for each agent.
Where it helps and where it fails
AI can assist monitoring (summarising error patterns) but cannot be its own overseer.

lessons.title: AI risks specific to insurance
lessons.outcome: Identify fairness, explainability, security, third-party and conduct risks in an AI use case.

blocks.text: Core ideas
Insurance is built on differentiating between risks, which makes the line between legitimate risk assessment and unfair discrimination central to AI governance. Six risk families matter most.

**Fairness and bias.** Models learn from historical data, which may reflect past unfair practices or under-representation of some groups. **Proxy discrimination** occurs when a variable that seems neutral, a location, a phone type, a mobile-money pattern, closely tracks a characteristic that should not drive decisions. **Explainability.** Customers declined, loaded or delayed are entitled to understand why; complex models can make this hard, and the IAIS treats transparency and explainability as a core supervisory topic (S07). **Robustness and security.** Models can fail on unusual inputs, degrade as conditions change (**model drift**), be manipulated (prompt injection, Unit 3.3), or leak sensitive data. **Third-party risk.** Most insurers will use vendor models and cloud platforms; the insurer remains accountable for outcomes, so contracts, data terms, audit rights and exit plans matter. **Conduct and customer outcomes.** AI that pushes products customers do not need, misstates cover, or makes claims harder to pursue creates conduct risk. **Over-reliance.** Staff may lose skills or stop challenging outputs (automation bias, Unit 2.2).
Regulation and practice

The EU AI Act classifies AI used for risk assessment and pricing of natural persons in life and health insurance as high-risk (S09); although not binding in Uganda, it signals where international expectations are heading and will apply to Ugandan firms serving EU-linked groups or clients. In Uganda, DPPA obligations apply to profiling and automated decisions (S05).
Scenarios from Ugandan insurance
These scenarios are illustrative. They have not yet been checked against interviews with practitioners.

A micro-health product uses an ML model to price cover. The model learns that customers in certain districts have higher claims; investigation shows those districts have better hospital access, so people there actually use their cover. Pricing on this pattern would penalise access to care rather than risk.
A vendor's chatbot for a broker stores conversations on overseas servers for "model improvement"; the contract does not address deletion or DPPA compliance.
Common mistakes

Assuming removing a protected attribute removes bias; accepting "the model is proprietary" as an answer to explainability questions; not monitoring after go-live; signing vendor terms without data and audit clauses.
Techniques to use

Ask of every use case: Who could be treated unfairly? Can we explain the outcome to the customer? What happens if it fails? Who is the vendor and what do they do with our data? How will we know if it drifts?

lessons.title: The governance landscape: IAIS, NIST, EU AI Act and Uganda
lessons.outcome: Apply this unit's method with evidence and accountable human review.

blocks.text: The governance landscape: IAIS, NIST, EU AI Act and Uganda

Welcome to The governance landscape: IAIS, NIST, EU AI Act and Uganda. This unit connects the concept to practical insurance work. As you listen, distinguish what a tool can prepare from the decisions a person must own. Every scenario is a teaching example, not an actual customer record or a promise that a feature is deployed.
Insurance supervision and organisational accountability

The International Association of Insurance Supervisors published an application paper on AI supervision in July 2025. It addresses proportionality, governance and accountability, robustness and security, transparency and explainability, and fairness and redress. Treat it as supervisory guidance, not an accreditation or an automatic finding that a product complies with Ugandan law. In a review, identify which risk is relevant, who owns it and what evidence supports the control.
A practical risk-management workflow

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework offers four connected functions. Govern establishes ownership and policy. Map describes context, affected people and risks. Measure tests and tracks relevant performance and risks. Manage prioritises and responds to the findings. An organisation can use these functions to structure its own review. A completed form is not proof that a control works; retain test results and the decision made from them.
Applicable law is a separate question

An insurer using AI must identify the laws, supervisory requirements and contractual obligations that apply to its actual activities and information processing. For Uganda, consult the current official data-protection instruments, insurance legislation and regulator material with the relevant legal or compliance owner. Do not infer that an activity is unregulated because there is no familiar AI-specific label. Avoid relying on an unverified section number, a proposal or a remembered regulatory deadline.
International links require an applicability review

A foreign framework can be a useful reference without being the law that governs a particular activity. The EU AI Act has its own territorial scope, system categories, exceptions and implementation dates. A firm with international operations needs a current applicability review rather than a blanket statement that every insurance AI tool is high-risk or that a customer location alone decides the answer. Use the current official text and record the reviewer, date and reasoning. This unit does not provide a definitive legal opinion or teach a fixed commencement date.
Work through a governance review

Consider a fictional insurer preparing claim summaries. The process owner describes the documents, users and intended result. The information-governance owner checks permitted processing and vendor terms. The reviewer tests the summaries against source documents and examines missing information, language errors and unsupported coverage statements. The manager decides whether the evidence justifies a bounded pilot and records conditions. A legal question that remains unresolved is assigned, not filled with an AI-generated answer.
Apply the distinction

Prepare a small table with four columns: source or framework, its role in your review, the evidence you need and the accountable owner. Separate a voluntary framework, international supervisory guidance, applicable law and the organisation's own policy. Name one question you cannot resolve from the supplied information and write the precise request you would send to the relevant owner. This makes the uncertainty actionable without pretending that the review itself grants approval.
Practise, check and apply

Before taking the quiz, write down the main idea in your own words. Apply it to a fictional task in your role, name the evidence needed and identify what you would check before anyone relies on the result. Keep unresolved questions visible and route decisions to the authorised person. Complete the ten-question quiz independently, then revisit any concept that needs more practice.

lessons.title: Assessing an AI use case end to end
lessons.outcome: Complete an AI use-case assessment canvas and recommend whether and how to proceed.

blocks.text: Core ideas

The **AI Use-Case Assessment Canvas** pulls together everything in the course into one page that a professional can bring to their manager, risk team or board. It has ten boxes: (1) **Problem and baseline**: what is going wrong today, in numbers; (2) **Proposed AI solution**: category (rules, ML, GenAI, agent) and what it does; (3) **Users and affected people**: staff who use it, customers affected; (4) **Data**: what data, whose, where it is processed, DPPA basis; (5) **Autonomy and decision rights**: level per action, what is never automated; (6) **Value**: expected benefit and how it will be measured; (7) **Risks**: fairness, explainability, security, third-party, conduct, over-reliance; (8) **Controls**: verification steps, escalation triggers, audit trail, monitoring, stop mechanism; (9) **Governance mapping**: IAIS topics and NIST functions addressed; (10) **Recommendation and pilot plan**: proceed, proceed with conditions, or do not proceed; scope, duration, success criteria, owner, review date.

A use case is not "approved" by filling in the canvas; the canvas makes the reasoning visible so the right people can decide. Proportionality applies: a GenAI tool drafting internal notes needs a short canvas; an agent interacting with customers needs a full one.
Regulation and practice

The canvas supports DPPA accountability (including any impact assessment the Regulations require for high-risk processing, to be confirmed) and demonstrates governance to the IRA. It should be stored with the approval decision and revisited at the review date.
Common mistakes
Leaving the baseline blank, so benefits cannot be shown; listing risks without matching controls; no named owner; no review date; treating the canvas as a one-off form.

blocks.text: A customer asks a simple question

A customer messages a branch or an insurance agent. They use a motorcycle for deliveries and want to understand what cover they might need. They ask you to reply in the same conversation. It sounds like a simple question. But before you answer, you need to understand the customer's situation, find the relevant product information, explain it accurately and know when to refer. Artificial intelligence can help prepare that work. In this unit, we follow this fictional enquiry through the customer journey and see which tasks A-I can assist with, and which responsibilities remain with people.
What you will be able to do

By the end, you should be able to do four things. First, describe the journey from an enquiry to ongoing service and renewal. Second, separate what the customer actually said from what a system has guessed. Third, check an A-I-prepared reply before a customer receives it. And fourth, prepare a handover that helps the next person act without making the customer repeat everything. The aim is practical: use A-I to improve preparation, while keeping each customer-facing action and each insurance decision with the right owner.
See the whole journey

Think of the journey as six stages. An enquiry arrives. Discovery clarifies the need and the facts still missing. Explanation helps the customer understand relevant information. Referral or application moves the case to the authorised process. Service handles questions and updates after that. A renewal review considers whether the customer's situation or the available terms have changed. Customers can move backwards or stop at any point. An application is not the same as confirmed cover. At each stage, record what has actually happened, what happens next and who is responsible.
Different channels, clear ownership

An enquiry may start with an agent, at a bank branch or in a service inbox. Several teams may help, but a customer should not have to work out the internal organisation chart. In a bank-and-insurer example, the branch prepares information and refers through its approved process. The authorised insurer team handles decisions within its role. Your own organisation must define these responsibilities. A-I can summarise the enquiry for the next person, but it cannot create authority that a person or system does not already have. A clear owner and next action matter more than a long automated conversation.
What is known, and what is missing?

Return to our fictional customer. We know that they use a motorcycle for deliveries, want an explanation and asked for a reply here. We do not know the applicable product, whether the use is eligible, the terms, the premium or whether they already have cover. A fluent system might fill these gaps with a plausible story. That would make the reply sound complete while weakening its accuracy. Keep unknowns visible. A customer statement is evidence of what they said. It is not proof that an insurer has accepted the risk or that a particular benefit applies.
Match the task to the tool

Not every useful task needs a complex agent. A fixed rule can route a new enquiry to a branch queue. A generative assistant can draft a summary or rewrite an approved explanation in clearer language. An agentic workflow may combine several preparation steps, such as finding the relevant source, collecting unanswered questions and preparing a handover. These are examples of possible designs, not a promise that every function exists in your current system. Choose the simplest tool that helps with the task. Then define what it can read, what it may prepare and what needs a person before anything changes or is sent.
Ground the explanation in the right source

For this exercise, imagine an approved training extract says that delivery use must be referred for confirmation and that terms depend on the insurer's review. That is the only product information we have. A useful draft must stay within it. It may explain that delivery use needs review and ask focused follow-up questions. It must not invent a premium, promise a claim payment or say that cover is already active. Save the source reference and its version with the draft so the reviewer can check the exact passage. If you cannot find support for a statement, remove it or refer the question.
Compare two replies

Compare two replies. Reply A says, you are covered for deliveries and all claims will be paid. It is short and confident, but neither statement is supported. Reply B says, I can help explain the options. Delivery use needs confirmation. May I ask a few questions before we refer it? Reply B moves the conversation forward while preserving uncertainty. It still needs review for the organisation's wording, the channel and the actual source. Clear communication is not a choice between sounding confident and saying nothing. You can give a useful next step without promising an outcome you cannot confirm.
Review before a customer-facing action

Before a prepared reply is sent, check five things. Is it for the right customer and enquiry? Does each product statement have supporting evidence? Is the channel appropriate for this contact and the organisation's current contact rules? Is the next step clear? And does the reviewer have authority to approve this action? Review should be a real opportunity to edit, return, stop or refer. A routine click that nobody has time to question adds little protection. If the wording is unsupported, correct it. If the source is missing, pause that claim. Do not turn the customer into the final quality checker.
A score helps organise work

A team may use a score or a worklist to organise follow-up. Treat it as a prompt to inspect the evidence, not as a conclusion about the customer. A high-priority enquiry is not automatically eligible for cover. A low-priority enquiry is not a rejection. Ask what the priority is based on, which facts are missing and whether the next action is appropriate. For our customer, a useful next action may simply be to clarify delivery use and prepare a referral. The quality of that action matters more than making a number look precise.
Make the handover useful

A useful handover contains the customer's stated need, the known facts, the unanswered questions, the source used, the current contact status and the next action with an owner. Our fictional note might say: customer requests an explanation for a motorcycle used in deliveries; eligibility and premium are unconfirmed; training extract requires referral; reply requested in this conversation; assigned officer to clarify the required details and refer. Keep irrelevant personal details out. The purpose is to help the next person verify and act. A long transcript alone is not a handover, and a summary without its supporting record is harder to check.
Handle service, renewal and stop requests

The same preparation discipline applies after an application. A service update should distinguish a recorded status from an expected outcome. A renewal conversation should check current terms and changed needs rather than assuming the previous arrangement continues. If a customer disputes a statement or asks for a person, route the issue with context. If they ask you to stop outreach, record that request and stop the relevant workflow under the organisation's procedure. Do not keep sending because the next message was already drafted. A-I can prepare a helpful update, but the workflow must respect the latest evidence and contact status.
Measure usefulness, not just activity

More messages do not automatically mean a better customer experience. Look at response time, whether handovers contain the required information, how often drafts need material correction and whether concerns or stop requests are handled properly. Commercial measures can be useful too, but define the population, period and denominator. Ten completed applications means something different out of twenty qualified enquiries than out of two thousand contacts. Compare like with like and check the quality of the outcome. For a small pilot, choose a few measures that the team can actually record and review before expanding the workflow.
Apply the checks, then take the quiz

Let us bring it together. Map the customer journey, keep facts separate from assumptions, ground product statements in the applicable source and assign the next action to the right person. Before you send, check the customer, wording, contact status, next step and authority. For your practice task, write a three-sentence reply to the fictional motorcycle enquiry and a short referral note. Use only the training facts supplied in this unit. Then take the ten-question quiz independently. The assessment is designed to hide the A-I assistant. In the next unit, we develop the discovery questions that help you understand the need without guessing.

blocks.text: Lead qualification and prioritisation

Welcome to Lead qualification and prioritisation. The learning goal is to choose the next follow-up using evidence without treating a worklist score as insurance eligibility. We will connect the method to a fictional insurance scenario, then ask you to prepare a work product you can check. The examples are not insurer product advice and do not establish that any feature is live.
Define the next action

Qualification asks whether there is enough relevant information and interest for a particular next step. It is not a promise that an insurer will accept the customer. Define the action first: clarify a missing fact, explain an option or refer an application. A record can be ready for clarification while still being unready for an application.
Use relevant evidence

A priority can reflect a stated need, requested timing, required missing information and the current contact status. Explain the reasons beside the priority. Do not infer affordability, eligibility or interest from an unrelated personal characteristic. Follow the approved method and flag missing information rather than using a precise-looking score to conceal it.
Apply contact status first

A customer who asked not to receive outreach does not become contactable because the lead looks valuable. Check contact status and permitted channel before preparing follow-up. Separate marketing follow-up from necessary service work under the organisation's procedure. Escalate unclear status rather than choosing the interpretation most likely to produce a sale.
Review the queue as work

A useful queue has a reason, owner and next action, not just a ranking. Review stale records, duplicated enquiries and changes in customer circumstances. Record why a priority changed. The officer can correct the ranking when the evidence changes, and the correction should remain traceable. A low follow-up priority is not a rejection of cover.
Work through the fictional case

Three fictional enquiries arrive. One asks for a callback today with the relevant details supplied. Another shows strong interest but asks to stop marketing contact. A third asks a general question and has not supplied the information needed for referral. Contact status prevents outreach to the second. Assign the first callback and prepare a clarification response for the third, using the authorised channel and review process.
Prepare the practical work

Create a worklist with evidence, missing facts, contact status, owner and next action. Explain why a priority is not an underwriting decision. Pause the lesson and create the work in your own words. Use fictional information. Where a source or fact is missing, mark it as unresolved rather than filling the gap with an assumption. Keep your first draft so that you can compare it with the checked version.
Review your work

Review your work in five passes. First, check each factual statement against the information supplied. Second, check that simplified wording has not changed the meaning. Third, check the intended recipient and whether the information is appropriate for them. Fourth, identify the authority required for any consequential action. Finally, make sure the next step has an owner and that unresolved questions remain visible. Record a correction you made and why it matters to the customer.
Compare an unsafe and a useful response

An unsafe work product can look complete because it substitutes certainty for missing evidence. A useful one says what is known, what remains unconfirmed and what an authorised person should do next. Apply that distinction to your own draft. If you have written that a policy is active, a price is final, a claim will be paid or an improvement is proven, identify the record that supports that statement. Remove or refer any conclusion that the source does not establish.
Your takeaways and independent quiz

The core outcome is to choose the next follow-up using evidence without treating a worklist score as insurance eligibility. Keep your completed practice work and the reasons for your corrections. Use the independent ten-question quiz to check your understanding. The unit is part of a broader course, so connect this method to the enquiry, service and review responsibilities you learned earlier. The assistant must not complete your assessment for you.
